explanations.explanation: Yes, baker, a palace for David. Hiram, king of Tyre, sent envoys, cedar logs, stonemasons and carpenters to build it (1 Chronicles 14:1). That's a whole crew sent for one palace. My mustache can pack a cookie box all day, but it cannot raise a roof.

I get why you'd think that, since cedar and builders sound like holy work. But the text says Hiram sent them "…to build a palace for him." meaning David (1 Chronicles 14:1). No temple is mentioned in this verse. Same crew, different blueprint.

A wall would be a fine use for all that wood, friend, but that's not what the verse says. Hiram sent stonemasons and carpenters along with the cedar logs "…to build a palace for him." (1 Chronicles 14:1). The only building named in this verse is David's palace.

That's it, baker. David realized the LORD had established him as king "…for the sake of His people Israel." (1 Chronicles 14:2). I love that he saw it that way. The kingdom wasn't about him showing off the new palace.

Close to the right neighborhood, but no. The verse says the LORD exalted David's kingdom "…for the sake of His people Israel." (1 Chronicles 14:2). Priests aren't mentioned there at all. It's the whole people.

An army feels like a kingdom word, I'll give you that. But the text says David's kingdom was highly exalted "…for the sake of His people Israel." (1 Chronicles 14:2). Nothing about soldiers in that verse.

Not quite, baker. The verse says the Philistines went in search of David, but David learned of this and "…went out to face them." (1 Chronicles 14:8). He didn't hide in the back of anything. Trust me, I know a thing or two about hiding, and David wasn't doing it.

Right, it's false. When the Philistines went searching for David, he learned of it and "…went out to face them." (1 Chronicles 14:8). No hiding, no waiting for them to go home. Picture me hearing trouble was looking for me. I'd be under the counter.

explanations.answer: He asks God what to do
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. David inquired of God: "Should I go up against the Philistines? Will You deliver them into my hand?" (1 Chronicles 14:10). He brought the question straight to God instead of guessing. I wish I'd asked my oven before I tried a batch with it turned off.

A sensible guess, since a leader might gather his people. But the text says David "…inquired of God…" (1 Chronicles 14:10). It doesn't mention him calling a meeting. The question he brought was for God: should he go up, and would God deliver them.

explanations.answer: He sends gifts to make peace
explanations.explanation: Nice try, but this was not a gift-basket moment. The Philistines had raided the valley, and David "…inquired of God…" whether he should go up against them (1 Chronicles 14:10). Nothing in the text about sending presents.
Yep, it's true. David asked, and the LORD replied, "Go," and then "for I will deliver them into your hand." (1 Chronicles 14:10). A clear yes and a promise. You don't get a better answer than that.

Actually it's true, friend. David asked, "Will You deliver them into my hand?" and the LORD replied, "Go," and then "for I will deliver them into your hand." (1 Chronicles 14:10). He got a clear yes and a promise, no maybe about it.

Not this time, baker. David said, "Like a bursting flood, God has burst out against my enemies by my hand." (1 Chronicles 14:11). He pointed to God, not to his men's courage. He even says it's God who burst out.

Right, it's false. David said, "Like a bursting flood, God has burst out against my enemies by my hand." (1 Chronicles 14:11). The credit went to God, and the place was named Baal-perazim after it. I'd have been tempted to put my own name on the cookie box.

Yes, their gods. The text says, "There the Philistines abandoned their gods…" (1 Chronicles 14:12). Walking away from your own gods is a big thing to do. I think that's a strange scene, and David had an order ready for them next.
Chariots would be a big thing to lose, I agree. But this passage doesn't mention any. It says, "There the Philistines abandoned their gods…" (1 Chronicles 14:12).

Not the king, baker. The verse says the Philistines "…abandoned their gods…" at Baal-perazim (1 Chronicles 14:12). That's the thing the text says they left. It names no king there, so hold on to the gods.
That's right. "…David ordered that they be burned in the fire." (1 Chronicles 14:12). He gave a clear order and that was that. No debating, no committee.
Burying sounds tidy, but that's not what the text says. David "…ordered that they be burned in the fire." (1 Chronicles 14:12). Fire, not dirt.
Returning them would be a very polite thing to do, but no. David "…ordered that they be burned in the fire." (1 Chronicles 14:12). They did not go back in a box with a bow on it.

Nope, baker. The text says "…David again inquired of God…" (1 Chronicles 14:14). One win didn't make him skip the asking. I once thought I knew a recipe by heart and made a cookie nobody could identify.
Right, false. "…David again inquired of God…" (1 Chronicles 14:14). Having won once, he asked again anyway. A smart move, since the second answer came with a brand new plan.

explanations.answer: Circle around and attack by the balsam trees
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. God said, "Do not march up after them, but circle around them and attack them in front of the balsam trees." (1 Chronicles 14:14). It's a different plan from the first battle, so I'm glad David asked again.

That's the one thing God told him NOT to do. He said, "Do not march up after them, but circle around them and attack them in front of the balsam trees." (1 Chronicles 14:14). Marching straight in would have skipped the plan.

explanations.answer: Wait for them back in Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: Waiting at home is a calm idea, but it isn't in the text. God said, "Do not march up after them, but circle around them and attack them in front of the balsam trees." (1 Chronicles 14:14). David was sent out to circle around.

Yes, baker. God said, "As soon as you hear the sound of marching in the tops of the balsam trees, move out to battle…" (1 Chronicles 14:15). Hear the sound, then go. It's like pulling a batch out the second the timer dings. The signal told David when.
That's the opposite, friend. God said, "As soon as you hear the sound of marching in the tops of the balsam trees, move out to battle…" (1 Chronicles 14:15). The sound meant go, not retreat.

Close, friend, but no. God said, "As soon as you hear the sound of marching in the tops of the balsam trees, move out to battle…" (1 Chronicles 14:15). David did listen for that sound first. But the signal set the timing, not the morning. Once he heard it, he was to go.

explanations.answer: God has gone out ahead of him
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. God said the sound would mean "…that God has gone out before you to strike the camp of the Philistines." (1 Chronicles 14:15). So the sound in the treetops was a sign that God was already on the move. David didn't have to guess when to go. He just had to listen for it.

Easy to guess, but that's not what God said. The marching sound would mean "…that God has gone out before you to strike the camp of the Philistines." (1 Chronicles 14:15). God was the one going ahead.

explanations.answer: His army is ready to fight
explanations.explanation: Makes sense on the surface, but God gave a different meaning. The sound would mean "…that God has gone out before you to strike the camp of the Philistines." (1 Chronicles 14:15). It was about God going first, not David's soldiers getting ready.
Yes, true. "…David did as God had commanded him…" (1 Chronicles 14:16). He followed the plan and the signal he was given. That's a baker who actually reads the recipe, which I'm still working on.
It's actually true, friend. The text says, "…David did as God had commanded him…" (1 Chronicles 14:16). He followed the plan, and they struck down the Philistine army from Gibeon to Gezer.

That's it, baker. The verse says "…the LORD caused all nations to fear him." (1 Chronicles 14:17). David's fame went out into every land, and the fear of the nations is what the text credits to the LORD. It wasn't a publicity campaign.

The fighting was real, I'll give you that: "…they struck down the army of the Philistines all the way from Gibeon to Gezer." (1 Chronicles 14:16). But about the nations, the verse says "…the LORD caused all nations to fear him." (1 Chronicles 14:17). The text credits the LORD for that fear.
No prophet shows up in this verse, baker. It says, "…the LORD caused all nations to fear him." (1 Chronicles 14:17). The LORD is the one doing it.
